Abrogate

/AB-ruh-gayt/ - the stress falls on AB · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Abrogate means to abolish or cancel, usually by official authority.

With one signature, the queen abrogated the nobles' ancient hunting privileges in the royal forest.

Worked Example

When the merged airline's new owners abrogated the profit-sharing pact with its regional partners, an arrangement that had steadied fares for a decade vanished overnight, and the small carriers learned of it from a two-line notice.

Abrogate is more formal and more sweeping than cancel: it names an authority using official power to kill a law, treaty, or standing arrangement. Notice its frame — someone with power abrogates a formal arrangement.

How Abrogate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

repeal

repeal: removes one statute by the normal lawmaking process

scrap

scrap: the informal, everyday word for junking a plan or rule

Antonyms

enact

enact: to make into law — the beginning abrogate ends

preserve

preserve: to keep an arrangement alive and untouched

How Strong Is It? — waive → repeal → abrogate

waive vs. abrogate

waive vs. abrogate: To waive a rule is far milder than to abrogate it: the rule is set aside for one case and lives on for every other.

repeal vs. abrogate

repeal vs. abrogate: Repeal stops a step short of abrogate: it removes one statute by the usual process, while abrogate sweeps a whole law or treaty aside by naked authority.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ab-

Prefix — ab-: away, off

Root — rog

Root — rog: to ask, to propose (Latin rogare)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending

Put it together

Put it together: Ab- (away) + rog- (to ask, to propose) + -ate = to propose away. In Rome a law was passed by asking the assembly — rogare — so abrogare was to ask them to take it back again: to un-make a law by the same authority that made it.

Use the root in a new word: derogatory

Use the root in a new word: derogatory: The coach benched two players for derogatory chants aimed at the visiting goalkeeper.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / legal

Reach for abrogate when an authority formally does away with a law, treaty, or standing arrangement — it is official power speaking. For everyday endings, cancel or scrap does the work. Keep its neighbors straight: annul (this unit) erases a thing as if it had never existed, and nullified (this unit) says it has been stripped of legal force.
